MR, ROCHE-OPPORTUNITY FOR MEMBERS TO ATTEND TRI-LEVEL GOVERNMENT CONFERENCE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all members of parliament.
Two days ago I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs if members of parliament could be accredited as observers at the national tri-level intergovernmental meeting to be held in Edmonton next week. This meeting is to be open to the press but closed to observers. The minister replied that observers could not attend because "there is just not sufficient room available."
Yesterday, I moved a motion that the government direct the planning secretariat to permit one member of each of the four parties in the House of Commons to be accredited as an official observer. This motion was blocked by the government supporters.
Following this action, I consulted with the management of the Macdonald Hotel in Edmonton, where the meeting is to be held, and I was informed that the extended Tonquin Room holds 1,100 people theatre-style or, for a dinner setting, 800 persons. The suggestion that four members of parliament could not be fitted into a room of such dimensions is ludicrous and underscores why I am raising this question of privilege.
The meeting next week will be the second national tri-level conference. It will deal with the super-problem of urbanization, considering such issues as management of growth, land use, housing, transportation and finance. These are problems that parliament as a whole has a responsibility to solve, not just the government. It is vital, and within our rights, for members of parliament to have first-hand information on the various points of view presented by all governments. If members of parliament are forced to rely on press reports we may get a picture that is incomplete, to say the least.
For example, the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary last July was open to observers. It is a good thing it was, for the day after the Calgary conference I was able to come back to the House and report to all members my impressions and evaluation of the conference which were quite at variance with the slick, co-operative image of the federal government conveyed by the communications media. That speech is reported on page 6054 of Hansard. If members of parliament had not had direct access to the western conference, we would not have known the full story.
Of course, the government does not want opposition members of parliament around when they are doing business. The record of this government has been one of continual downgrading and diminishment of the role of the member.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to report to hon. members on my visit to China which, as the House knows, concluded just a few hours ago.
The invitation to me to visit the People's Republic of China was first extended by Premier Chou En-lai in 1971 and was renewed again several months ago.
We left Canada with high expectations. I am able to say, Mr. Speaker, that the willingness of the Chinese government to accept our point of view and to engage with us in activities of benefit for the people of Canada more than met those expectations. The high degree of interest of the Chinese government in Canada and the willingness of that government to work toward the maintenance and strengthening of friendly relations with Canada were made evident by the amount of time they, the Chinese leaders, were willing to devote to me and to my party. Chairman Mao Tse-tung extended to me the courtesy of a long conversation. Premier Chou En-lai met with me for many hours of formal discussions over the course of several days and chatted with me at even greater length in informal circumstances on a number of occasions.
One of the main objectives of any visit by a head of government, whether a Canadian travelling abroad, or a prime minister coming here, is to ensure that each country understands the policies of the other and the circumstances which give rise to those policies. It is seldom possible to come to agreement on the wisdom or the effectiveness of all policies, nor would one expect that this

could be the case in a world in which the vagaries of history, the realities of geography, and the variations of social systems lend distinctive directions and points of view to governmental policies. What I found most heartening, however, in my discussions with the Chinese leaders, was their understanding of, and sympathy for, Canada's foreign policy. In particular I was not subjected to any demands that future Canadian relations with China would depend for their warmth on our attitudes toward any other country. I stated in Peking, both in the privacy of conversation with the Premier and on public occasions, that Canadian foreign policy seeks to avoid tension, to strengthen the institutions of international cooperation and to assist the economic development of the newly independent countries. I said as well that, in my belief, the true measurement of national greatness was found not in military might or in political hegemony but in the willingness of a country to recognize the importance of individual welfare, human dignity and a sense of personal accomplishment and fulfilment.
Many of the issues which were discussed with the Chinese leaders, and in the several committees of officials that were established during the course of the visit, reflected these beliefs and the desire of Canada to expand its international trade.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, Premier Chou and I signed a formal trade agreement which will serve as a framework for the development of trade between Canada and China for the next three years. I should like to table now, in both official languages, copies of this agreement.
Hon. members will find that this agreement established a joint trade committee which will meet annually. The Canadian suggestion that the committee address itself immediately to the areas of transportation, forestry and agriculture, was accepted by the Chinese. Agreement was reached as well that detailed discussions be initiated quickly in the fields of aluminum and wood pulp. We also agreed that further discussions take place soon with respect to potash, sulphur and nickel. The Canadian side was heartened by the obvious Chinese interest in increasing the purchase of Canadian manufactured goods and contemplating the purchase from Canada of complete plants. Throughout our discussions in this area, emphasis was lent by both sides of the mutual benefit to be gained from long-term commercial agreements.
Satisfying as were the discussions on trade and commercial relations, I was moved most by the several understandings reached in the areas of medicine and human relations. Hon. members will be familiar with the important work done last spring in China by a joint governmental and professional medical mission to China led by Dr. Gustave Gingras, the then President of the Canadian Medical Association. That mission recognized the immense benefits that could be realized in health care services in Canada if more were known about several areas of Chinese medical techniques. The hope was subsequently expressed by the two major medical bodies in Canada that the Canadian government attempt to encourage the Chinese to engage in co-operative activities with Canadian doctors to these ends.
October 19, 1973

I am delighted in the progress that we were able to make in this respect during my visit, which provides for teams of Canadian and Chinese physicians visiting one another's countries to study advanced techniques in each place. The field of interest chosen by Canadian doctors in this first phase is that of acupuncture analgesia. I am informed that if this technique proves as successful in the Canadian social environment as has been the case in China, its contributions in the elimination of anaesthetic complications, in the reduction of costs associated with surgery, and in the extension of surgery to elderly and high-risk patients now denied treatment, will rank it as one of the major contributions to Canadian medicine.
I am particularly appreciative of the willingness of Premier Chou to agree to my request that facilities be instituted which will lead to the reunion of families. Just as I regarded this question of reunification as one of the most important of the subjects in which I engaged Premier Kosygin in discussion-and which has since led to the exit from the Soviet Union of several hundreds of persons to join relatives in Canada-so I emphasized to Premier Chou the importance with which Canadians as a whole viewed this aspect of Canadian-Chinese relations.
I have instructed Canadian officials to waste no time in the implementation of this new understanding which permits Canadian immigration officers to proceed to China to process applicants for entry to Canada. An officer of the Department of Manpower and Immigration is already on his way from Ottawa to Peking.
Understandings were reached in other fields as well: cultural and sports exchanges, for one, consular arrangements for another, and science and technology for still another. The latter was made possible by the extensive work done in advance of my arrival by the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
My visit to China, Mr. Speaker, leaves me without any doubt of the wisdom of the decision of the Canadian government to reverse the longstanding policy of ignoring the People's Republic of China.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
Because that immense country of talented and industrious people will have an increasing impact on world affairs, and because a strengthening and enrichment of the bilateral relationship between Canada and China can be beneficial to Canadians, that decision was right and will increasingly prove to be right. The presence of China in the United Nations and in other international councils makes it vital that Canada's interests and Canada's views be understood and, hopefully, supported by the Chinese government. It will be of increasing advantage to Canada that Canadian leaders have opportunities to explain Canadian attitudes and policies to Chinese decision-makers just as, amongst other things, I exposed to Premier Chou the positions Canada will advocate at the forthcoming Law of the Sea Conference.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I was heartened again and again by the genuine friendship
Visit by Prime Minister to China extended toward Canada and Canadians by the leaders and the people of modern China. I am confident that the diversification and enjoyment of our new ties with China will not interfere with the longstanding friendly relations which we enjoy with those several countries with which we have special ties. Nor will it detract from our efforts to seek, to our advantage, the easing of tensions and the increase of contacts with other parts of the world.
It has not been the vastness of the Pacific that has acted as a barrier between Canada and China. The gulf has been found all too often in the minds of those of us who are unwilling to recognize the magnitude of one of the most significant revolutions in the history of the world and the extension of basic human amenities to hundreds of millions of persons to whom they had been denied for millennia.
The name of Canada is held in high respect in China, Mr. Speaker, and as a consequence Canadians are beneficiaries. It is the aim of this government that this reputation, and those benefits, increase and continue.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before commenting specifically on the visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to China I should like to take this occasion to congratulate him belatedly on his birthday.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the good wishes of the House on the Prime Minister's birthday are really quite relevant to any discussion of the China visit because of the right hon. gentleman's published tributes to the aging leaders of that centuries old society. The Prime Minister is quoted as saying in regard to this aging leadership: "It is this kind of faith that leaves me full of admiration when I see these really aging leaders prepared to begin all over again." Along these lines, Mr. Speaker, I feel obliged to remind the Prime Minister that, while he has had another birthday, I am still older than he is. Of course, I am doubly pleased that the Prime Minister's remarks indicated an appreciation of all leaders who are capable of beginning all over again. Here again, I might claim membership in that club.
When I visited China in 1971 it was a wonderful, illuminating and fascinating experience, but I encountered somewhat the same difficulty that I faced on a visit to the Soviet Union in 1970. This related to clarifying my position as Leader of the Opposition. I found on both occasions that, while I was most hospitably received, within the systems of government operating in those states an identifiable and active leader of the opposition was a rather foreign concept. I came to understand that in certain parts of the world it was accepted that by the time you found out there was an effective opposition, it was perhaps too late. The relevance of this observation to the contemporary Canadian scene is perhaps, I think, self-evident.

Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
The exchanges of people and ideas in the areas of medical science, health care technology, culture, education, sports and the media should be very beneficial. There is much that we can learn from one another. There is no doubt about that. In the technique of acupuncture alone we have already seen remarkable results in Canada. Just look at what it has done for the Ottawa Rough Riders.
Our economic and diplomatic relations with the Peoples Republic of China are only beginning to develop fully and to offer significant potential benefit to our country. I feel it is helpful and timely that the Prime Minister, the head of our government, participate directly at this stage of the relationship. Therefore I offer the Prime Minister my congratulations on his visit.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
I feel that the visit further demonstrated that our two countries are building friendly and constructive relationships and that Canada has a growing commitment to expand its activities on the Pacific rim.
I am sure that all Canadians were pleased to learn of the various projects between our two countries that were formally announced during the Prime Minister's visit to China. With regard to trade and economics, we welcome the agreement establishing a joint trade committee which will meet annually. The understanding of both governments to increase and widen trade between our two countries can be of great importance. Interchanges suggested by the Prime Minister in the areas of transportation, forestry and agriculture are certainly appropriate. However, the agreement really only establishes a framework to develop our trading opportunities. It provides a challenge to Canada and should be seen in that light.
While we expect a significant increase in the volume of trade with China next year and have long supported the continued growth of our wheat exports, Canadian trade with China, and with everyone else for that matter, must involve a far greater proportion of manufactured products. We are faced with extremely energetic competition in this new market. If we are to realize our true potential with regard to China, decisive strategic leadership must be taken at home. Any effective long-term trade relationship with another country must also be a two-way relationship. With that in mind we accept that part of the agreement, of course, which extends most- favoured-nation tariff treatment to Chinese goods entering Canada. This is realistic and quite equitable, because it should be pointed out that Chinese sales to Canada totalled only about $48 million last year, less than one-fifth of our sales to China.
I touch on only one disturbing note, Sir. There was no mention in the Prime Minister's remarks today or in his Peking communique of nuclear bomb testing in China. I would sincerely hope that our new relationships as well as our older ones would permit us to be prepared to be frank and open on matters of Canadian and world-wide concern. I felt that we were less emphatic than we might have been in our protests to the French government over their latest test series. I hope the Prime Minister will be able to give the House some assurance that he did convey to the

Chinese leaders the very deep concern of the Canadian people about continued nuclear bomb testing.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON HIS VISIT TO CHINA
speechtext:
I do not wish to be misunderstood, Sir. I repeat what I have said in the past: The comments of Canadian leaders on sensitive issues do not have to be rude or offensive, and I do not expect them to be, but they must be firm, they must be unequivocal and, most important, they must be made.
In the consular field we welcome the simplification of visa procedures and the provision for each country to set up a consulate general in the other country. I welcome fully with the Prime Minister the fact that it will now be possible for the Canadian government to process within China applications for the reunion of families. This, of course, is of deep concern to many Canadians, and I trust this long hoped for opportunity will be acted on energetically and as a high priority.
I again congratulate the Prime Minister. I am pleased to see that the Prime Minister and Mrs. Trudeau have completed their long journey and returned home in good health.

speechtext:
What this trip and what the last two or three years indicate is the unwisdom of Canada and other countries in having refused to recognize the Peking government of China for so many years. As every member of this House knows, my party has been advocating that recognition since 1950. I think the value of recognizing a large country, despite the disagreements we may have with some aspects of the social system there, has been fully justified by what has happened, culminating in the trip the Prime Minister has just made to that country. I
October 19, 1973

express the hope that other countries, particularly our powerful neighbour to the south, will see that any attempt to isolate any country, large or small but particularly an important country like China, is harmful to the future of the world and to the relationships that must be developed in the world. I look forward, if I may say this as a Canadian without trying to interfere, to the day, I hope soon, when the United States of America will also recognize China. We will then have a situation in the United Nations in which no one fails to recognize the importance and place of the Chinese Republic in the present world situation.
The modern world, Mr. Speaker, has produced new problems as a result of technological and industrial development and it has inevitably produced different social systems and different social ideas. One absolute precondition for peace in the world and for the possibility of the world's continued growth and development is that all of us must accept the fact that there are differing social systems and differing social ideas in this world and not make them an issue for war or conflict or a refusal to deal with each other as citizens of the world.
I note that toward the end of the Prime Minister's statement there is a very important sentence which may have escaped the attention of hon. members. I congratulate the Prime Minister on using these words:
The gulf has been found all too often in the minds of those of us who are unwilling to recognize the magnitude of one of the most significant revolutions in the history of the world-
Note the following words, Mr. Speaker:
-and the extension of basic human amenities to hundreds of millions of persons to whom they had been denied for millennia.
I take from those words a recognition that the government and the people of China is doing its best in its way to improve the standard of life of its people, and the Prime Minister congratulates them for the progress they have made and wishes them well in future. As a fellow Canadian I join him in those congratulations and in those wishes.
The Leader of the Opposition has dealt with most of the important, relevant details of the agreements as set out in the statement, all of which my colleagues and I support wholeheartedly as, indeed, did the Leader of the Opposition. There are times, Sir, when partisanship is pushed aside, and those times are probably the best in the history of our parliament.
I want to say this in conclusion. No one in Canada who knows anything about foreign affairs has ever had any illusion that our country can play the role of superpower, can play the role of imposing ideas on any part of the world, or that we are able, because of our economic and military power, to push people in a right or wrong direction as we see our interests to be. No one has ever had that kind of illusion about Canada's role. But some Canadians underestimate the role that Canada can play. Canada is an important middle power. Canada has a history without any colonial connections. Canada has a history of supporting all peoples around the world seeking independence and freedom. Canada has no black pages in its history of colonizing people or exploiting them from the centre of some imperial power. Because it is a middle power, because it has that happy history, Canada can play a significant role in relations among the governments and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. members who have just spoken, I am glad to see the right hon. Prime Minister returning in such great form.
We are happy to see him and Mrs. Trudeau in perfect health and happy after an excellent journey.
May I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the Prime Minister on his birthday. We have something in common: we are both Libra. As there is a two year difference between us, he must certainly be older than I am. Being both Libra probably means that we are the two better balanced hon. members in the House.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's statement certainly gives us food for thought. Approximately twelve years ago, I heard about and read a book entitled "Two Innocents in China". As I was reading a few days ago about one of these innocents who had certainly never expected to return as Prime Minister of Canada, I could somewhat envision what had happened previously.
Mr. Speaker, here is what riveted my attention and which makes sense in the Prime Minister's statement.
I said as well that, in my belief, the true measurement of national greatness was found not in military might as in political hegemony, but in the willingness of a country to recognize the importance of individual welfare, human dignity and a sense of personal accomplishment and fulfilment.
Those thoughts should be pondered over not only in Canada but also in other countries.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister then stated that trade agreements have been concluded with China. He said, for example, that the Canadian delegates noted, to their great satisfaction, that the Chinese were anxious to increase their purchases of Canadian manufactured goods and that they were considering the purchase in Canada of complete industrial facilities. Throughout those talks, emphasis was laid on both sides on the mutual advantages of long-term trade agreements. In my opinion, it would now be necessary to know exactly what we could exchange with the Chinese from the technical or technological point of view. But the cultural and scientific agreements are quite valuable; they will greatly help Canadians learn about China and the Chinese to learn about Canada. Acupuncture, which was a laughing subject for years, and which is now considered with greater attention and seriousness in Canada, is mentioned here. Moreover, the Prime Minister says that some Canadians have ensured him, and I quote:
-that if this technique proves as successful in the Canadian social environment as has been the case in China, its contributions in the elimination of anaesthetic complications, in the reduction of costs associated with surgery will be remarkable-
Mr. Speaker, these are essential points, and when I was questioned during the Prime Minister's visit in China, I answered unequivocally that not only did I not object, but that I would also encourage these scientific, technological

Visit by Prime Minister to China and cultural exchanges which could increase not only our own knowledge but also that of other people.
However, I did find the following comments, which have also been mentioned by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis), somewhat revolutionary, and I quote:
It has not been the vastness of the Pacific that has acted as a barrier between Canada and China. The gulf has been found all too often in the minds of those of us who were unwilling to recognize the magnitude of one of the most significant revolutions in the history of the world and the extension of basic human amenities to hundreds of millions of persons to whom they had been denied for millennia.
I am rather skeptic about these remarks contained in the Prime Minister's statement. The Prime Minister did certainly not see a parliamentary system like ours in China. There are no leaders of the opposition in China like there are here. There is no freedom such as ours in China. I therefore think that it is a bit much to praise a revolution because the country which made it is large. This is the same as saying: We are happy about what happened in Cuba and Czechoslovakia. We welcomed the events which took place in Chile and China. If we consider what is happening closer to home we would be glad to have the separatists controlling the province of Quebec for the very same reasons as those mentioned in this statement!
The freedom of speech and action we are enjoying in Canada must be respected and we should not yield to anybody through any system imposed forcefully through revolution while there is so much room for agreement, comprehension and co-operation.
I do not accept the Quebec separatists nor their spirit of revolution and the violence they use and I will never approve violence in any country whether it be China or Russia. Even though the Prime Minister's visit was beneficial in certain areas, if we must recognize a forcefully imposed political system I disagree. For instance I agree in the case of-

Certainly, the very same thing happened in Chile. When it happened in Cuba our NDP friends did not object. When communists are responsible for bloody revolutions, they are applauded by Canadian socialists.
Mr. Speaker, I have seldom seen liars of this kind. In Parliament we are shown a window display but they do quite the reverse outside.
When I mention revolutions it is to state clearly that I object to them and when I say that we should not encourage those revolutions in Quebec-they raise fear throughout Canada.
Should the Prime Minister say: At last, Quebec which has been misunderstood would do well to separate from the rest of Canada because since Confederation it has been under the tutelage of the federal government, we would not accept that.
Mr. Speaker, I believe in exchanges while having our identity respected, but our identity is characterized by freedom which allows us to breathe freely as human beings can and must do in the world.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE REGULATIONS- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 43 to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that a large number of Newfoundland's inshore fishermen are adversely affected by the existing Unemployment Insurance Commission regulations, and in view of the federal government's obvious lack of concern and understanding for this problem, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall):
That the Ministers of Manpower and Fisheries, in their collaboration in working out changes to the existing Unemployment Insurance Commission regulations as they apply to fishermen, be instructed by this House to adopt the recommendations of the Newfoundland Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers Union which are as follows:

However, I believe that the figures I have given demonstrate that is not true. Not only is it not true, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is interesting to review what is happening in certain countries that have removed the death penalty or partially removed it.
The United Kingdom is often mentioned by the government as a country that has abolished the death penalty and they suggest that we should follow its example. But yesterday I commented that in the United Kingdom there are serious second thoughts about the matter. I would also point out that at the recent Conservative conference in that country the matter was raised and, by a vote of 1,404 in favour and 1,228 against, the motion was carried for the restoration of the death penalty.
The United Kingdom is not the only country showing a definite trend back to the death penalty. Our nearest

neighbour, the United States, is having serious misgivings concerning the abolitionist stance in many of the states and of the federal jurisdiction itself. Last week I had an opportunity to attend a conference in Washington, D.C. which was called to consider peace in the world. I think it is most significant that I was warned not to risk walking the streets of Washington alone at night. I was told that if I were to walk from the conference hall to my hotel for example, I stood a 50-50 chance of being mugged. That is the atmosphere of which I believe this government is not properly cognizant.
There is, to a certain extent, a rising trend of violence and murder. I think it is interesting to look at the situation in the state of California which has a population approximately equal to that of Canada. That state experimented with abolition of the death penalty for murder. It is interesting to note that, unlike this government, the state of California decided to ask the people for their verdict on whether the death penalty should be restored. In the referendum conducted last year, the people voted by approximately 57 per cent to restore the death penalty in that state.
In this connection I will be interested to know if the Solicitor General has actively discussed with his counterparts of the governments of the various states of the United States of America, and with his counterpart in the federal government of the United States, the concerns and attitudes respecting the continuation or restoration of the death penalty in that country. I say that because I think it might be interesting to review some testimony given by the Attorney General of the State of California. He testified before the legislature of the state in support of a bill for restoring the death penalty. For example, the Attorney General was asked, "Is the death penalty a deterrent?" His reply was:
Yes. The rise in the homicide rate during the last ten years, the experience of jurists and persons in law enforcement, and common sense indicate that it is.
Then, he broke his answer into three separate parts. Dealing with homicide, he pointed out that from 1956 to 1962, there were between five and eleven executions per year in California. During that time the wilful homicide rate fluctuated between 3.5 and 3.7 wilful homicides per
100,000	persons. Then, he said that since 1962, when the courts effectively abolished the death penalty in California, with the exception of one execution in 1967, the wilful homicide rate in California increased to 8.7 wilful homicides per 10,000 persons. I mention these figures because it is alarming to note that the same trends have appeared in Canada as a result of the death penalty not being imposed for murder. As I said when speaking during the second reading debate on this bill, murder statistics for Canada for 1971 demonstrate that the rate of murder in this country has more than doubled since 1956 and now stands at 2.4 per 100,000 persons.
The Attorney General of California went on to point out that jurists and law enforcement officials have repeatedly come into contact with individuals who have stated that they did not carry a weapon, or that they carried an unloaded weapon, because of fear of the death penalty. He then mentioned that he felt it is just common sense to
Capital Punishment
accept that the death penalty is a deterrent. He testified that this inference is substantiated by the fact that in 1960 there was one robbery-murder for every 300 robberies, while in 1972 the rate had increased to one robbery-murder for every 200 robberies.
The state of California chose to ask the people of the state what they desired with respect to the restoration of the death penalty. The people voted overwhelmingly in favour of the restoration of the death penalty. According to the returns on Proposition 17, the title given to the referendum, 5,386,904 Californians said, "Return to death penalty", whereas 2,591,547 persons said, "Do not restore it". That proportion supporting the restoration of the death penalty in California, I suggest, is very similar to the proportion of people in Canada, who would favour the restoration of the death penalty.
I have already referred to the Gallup poll of Canada which last year indicated that 63 per cent of the people in this country favoured the restoration of the death penalty. It is interesting to note that the percentage in favour of restoration last year was substantially higher than the percentage which was in favour of restoring the death penalty in 1966. At that time only 53 per cent asked for the death penalty to be retained, whereas it is clear that the percentage in favour of retention has risen by 10 per cent in the intervening five or six years.
The government ought to take cognizance of what the people of Canada are asking. Why can we not trust the people, and at least delay the railroading of this bill through Parliament, so that the law may be restored to its former status or left as it is at present. In the next election, which hopefully will come soon, the people of Canada, in addition to voting for those who are to represent them in this House, could also be asked to vote on the question of the continuation or abolition of capital pubish-ment in this country.
It is unfortunate that we in this country tend to react rather than give leadership. Surely, we do not need to wait until other countries in the world restore the death penalty before finding ourselves totally out of step. I feel I am representing my constituents well when I support the restoration of the death penalty in Canada. I took it upon myself to ascertain the wishes of my constituents, and I polled them. I point out that 89.4 per cent of those responding to that poll we conducted in York-Simcoe asked for the death penalty to be restored or retained.
If we vote in support of this bill today, we will regret it in future years. I urge members of the House either not to vote in support of the bill or, perhaps better still, if they support it, to change their vote, so that we are not put into the position in which criminals of this country will begin to regard the death penalty as the ultimate punishment to which they can be subjected if they do not obey the laws of the land.

Mr. Speaker, prior to the luncheon break I was saying that I felt the government, in sponsoring this bill, was out of step with many of the countries of the world and that in fact we were not taking a lead in going the way many abolitionist countries and states in the United States are tending to go, that is back to the institution of the death penalty.
Referring to the state of California, I think it is interesting to note that not only have they had a plebiscite which indicated by 67.5 per cent that the public in California felt the death penalty should be restored, but that state in fact brought in legislation that goes surprisingly far in restoring the death penalty for various crimes. 1 wish to summarize the crimes for which the state of California now imposes capital punishment as a result of a recent bill introduced in that House. One point that is made is that the death penalty should be for those killers and those crimes on which California juries actually and unconditionally returned death verdicts. Their bill provides that the basis for the death verdict must be first, that a homicide has been committed, that the killer has been sentenced to death and that he must have personally caused the act which caused the death, unless he contracted for the murder.
It is interesting to note that in the courts of California the process for the handling of murder trials is significantly different. It is a two level type of trial in which the man is found guilty or not guilty at the first level. If he is found guilty, there is an entirely new trial to determine if the facts dictate the mandatory imposition of the death penalty.
The California act will apply first to first degree murder if the victim is a peace officer and, second, if the victim was a witness to the crime and killed to prevent his testimony. The California governing officials have found instances where a person charged with a crime has admitted that he killed his victim because he realized the victim could testify against him. He knew there was no worse punishment in the then existing laws of California if he killed the man compared with the punishment for whatever crime he had committed. To cover that, the state has now provided for the death penalty where the victim was a witness to the crime and was killed in order to prevent him testifying against the accused.
California has also instituted the death penalty in the case of a multiple murder or of a person who has prior murder convictions. It has been instituted where there has been a history of two or more separate convictions for violent criminal conduct. If there is a first degree murder, they have instituted it if the accused was killed by torture. Finally, it is instituted in the case of first degree murder if it is felt that the accused is not rehabilitable and there are no mitigating circumstances.
In addition, the California act applies where a prisoner under life sentence kills another. It applies to skyjacking if any victim of the skyjacking should die. It applies to kidnapping for ransom, robbery, etc., if the victim dies. Finally, the act in California applies if a train wrecker causes victims to die as a result of a train derailment or

the wrecking of some mode of transportation. I remind hon. members that the state of California has found it necessary to institute such a wide return to the death penalty because, as the Attorney General indicated that, although a few short years ago he was an abolitionist, it was believed that the abolitionist stand resulted in a significantly higher homicide rate in that state than existed in prior years. I would remind hon. members of the facts that he brought out. In 1963, the homicide rate in California was 3.8 per 100,000 population, while in 1971 it had reached 8.1 per 100,000 population. As I indicated earlier today, by 1972 the rate had gone even higher in that state.
In short, the people of California asked that something be done. They were given an opportunity to reflect their wishes in the plebiscite to which I referred earlier. Sixty seven and a half per cent of them said the state should restore the death penalty, and the state legislature has met their wishes.
However, the government of Canada has refused to acknowledge the popular will of the vast majority of Canadians concerning the same subject. I believe that when we consider this matter we should realize that, while it is nice to take trips to China, to Russia and to certain other Communist countries, we will not find in those countries the lenient attitude towards the death penalty which this government feels is the proper attitude to take in Canada.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the people in my riding as well as in the province of Quebec and Canada in general are concerned with the increasing rise in crime in Canada. Not only are we experiencing a rapid increase in the rate of unemployment, the rate of inflation, but also a simultaneous increase in the number of crimes in Canada, and that is of great concern to the population. It seems that the softening of our laws and the tendency of federal and provincial authorities in matters of justice and crime

October 19, 1973
Capital Punishment
repression have in a certain way promoted the rise in crime in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I was completely baffled when I read the evidence given on April 27, 1972, before the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs by Mr. Justice Ciale of the Criminology Centre of the University of Ottawa where he stated that in 1967, according to the last comprehensive statistics available, 1,229,000 crimes were committed in Canada. Of course, those are not murders, Mr. Speaker, but crimes and the figure of 1,229,000 must be considered seriously. Those are crimes made known to police departments; how many others were not reported, how many others are in a certain way legalized? We are sometimes inclined to say that the worst criminals are not always behind bars.
Mr. Speaker, in his testimony Mr. Ciale said the following and I quote:
-with approximately 7,000 inmates in the penitentiary who have gone through the entire criminal justice system including the corrections stream. This is approximately one-fifth of one per cent in terms of crimes committed. So we have over one million crimes, but only about 7,000 people wind up in Canadian penitentiaries.
Mr. Speaker, a very small number of criminals are punished and I feel more and more strongly that they know it. I also believe that police authorities may have had orders not to search too much for criminals for if they were all arrested, we would have no place for them. And although we recently built prisons that look very much like palaces, it remains that the available space is nevertheless limited and the prospect of having to provide for prisoners' needs is disturbing for Canadian taxpayers.
We say that the big criminal or murderer doe not start at the top; he begins with larceny. If he is not punished, he gets worse and worse.
I was reading reports from the United States. For instance, in the March 7, 1973 edition of La Presse, one can read the following, and I quote;
The legislative assemblies of two thirds of the 50 states of the United States of America are considering the establishment of capital punishment and in four other states, the legislators already passed laws to restore capital punishment.
The United States Supreme Court decided last July, with respect to cases concerning Georgia and Texas, that capital punishment, as applied in most states, was unconstitutional. The ruling that was passed, the vote being five against four, nevertheless leaves the door open for the establishment of capital punishment, provided that the latter be uniformly applied.

Tn 1972, there were 18,520 murders committed in the United States (900 more than in 1971), and 54 percent were committed by means of handguns. One hundred and eight policemen were shot

with firearms. Nearly 100,000 people were threatened with a handgun, and 245,000 armed robberies were committed.
To this first group of figures, let us quickly add a second one. Each year, 1,800,000 Americans purchase a handgun. The national figure for handguns is about 30 million. To which we must add more than 60 million guns of all sizes.
Nearly one out of every two Americans has the means to kill his family, his neighbours, a stranger or himself. In the single week between March 4 and 11, 1973, 325 people were killed. And we make our young people believe by all sorts of means that once their studies are finished, they will get all opportunities to earn their living. Mr. Speaker, I think that we should restore the death penalty not for any case, but to punish capital murder, according to the provisions of the 1961 amendments. In my opinion, the danger of making a mistake is rather remote.

Oh, then he believes he is wrong. Right is wrong. That is an example of the double talk which you get from this minister and, indeed, from the government in general. The point is that there is no death penalty that can be devised which would do any good for the victim. It is not logical to say: let us abolish the death penalty because it does nothing for the victim, and at the same time not abolish any death penalty. What good does it do the victim to incarcerate the murderer in a penitentiary? Is the NDP advocating that we abolish the penitentiary services? The point is that the death penalty would not only be a punishment of the murderer but a demonstration of society's abhorrence of the crime of murder, and society's serious concern about this threat to public security. Society would be saying to the family of the survivors of the homicide act that we share with them in the devastation, in the tragedy that they have suffered, and we show our abhorrence by demanding that he who has callously taken the life of another shall be prepared to forfeit his own.
I suggest that, as we are practising the law in Canada, we are not demonstrating that to the families and loved ones of the victims of murder. We are sending murderers
Capital Punishment
into penitentiaries, not for a life sentence-we use the term "life sentence" in a euphemistic way meaning that we will send them there for ten years before letting them out on parole-but for a much shorter time after which they can be permitted to go out on temporary absence or day parole. It is possible for a murderer, after a short time in penitentiary, to be allowed out on a temporary absence or day parole so that he can go to university at public expense and enjoy the life of a university student, the life of a campus community. At the same time, however, the family and survivors of the victim of his homicidal act are deprived of the one who was their breadwinner, their father, their husband, the one who was the guardian of the home. That is the attitude that we are showing as a society. That is what we are saying to the family of a policeman struck down by a murderer. We are saying that we will not do anything more to the murderer than give him the opportunity to advance himself.
I submit to you that when we ask the question what good does it do the victim, we should be asking: what good will any penalty do? We have to have a penalty that will demonstrate to the whole of society, as well as to the criminal element, that society has this kind of abhorrence for the crime of murder.
The second point that has been made in this debate by a number of speakers is that they cannot support capital punishment because they believe that life is sacred. This has certainly been a strong point strongly made. But if we believe it consistently, we should ask ourselves: how is it that we vote for Bill C-2 which provides at least the legislative authority for the capital punishment of the murderers of prison guards and police officers. If we are opposed to capital punishment in principle so that we deny the right of the state ever to take a life, how can we possibly, consistently and logically support this bill?
Moreover, how can we support many of the other measures that we endorse in parliament which lead, at least potentially, to the possibility of the state taking human life? How can we support a budget in excess of $2 billion for the armed forces which have the potential for taking human life on a grand scale? We are concerned about the principle involved in the possible taking of life of one, two, three, four or five murderers, but here we are supporting the equipment of the armed forces which could take thousands of lives. Similarly, how is it that we support arming the police forces across this country, all of them having the potential for taking life in the line of duty and in the interests of protecting society? How can we support putting shotguns into the hands of prison guards on the perimeter walls and on the watch towers? How can we give them the means by which they can take the life of an escaping inmate for the great crime of attempting escape from an institution? I am not suggesting that any prison guard would deliberately take the life of an escapee, but it certainly could happen with the use of a shotgun. We would say that, should it happen, a guard would certainly be excused the act since it was committed in the line of duty.
If we are thus supporting all these things-and I think it is right that we as parliament should support them-are we not saying that the state has the right and the authority under the circumstances to take life? It seems to me

October 19, 1973
Capital Punishment
that we are logical and consistent only if we take the thoroughgoing pacifist position of saying that the state never has the right under any circumstances to take life. Then, we have to ask serious questions about the state's right to take life in other circumstances, namely in time of war or in the exercise of a policeman's duty.
A third argument that has been advanced in this debate is that capital punishment is too extreme a penalty for society to exact because the courts, being human, are fallible-judges make mistakes and juries make mistakes. There is always the danger of the innocent being convicted and executed. I find this to be a very strong argument. I must say that I am deeply impressed by the need for society to take the utmost care that no innocent person be convicted of a crime and sentenced to death.
However, let us recognize certain other aspects of this point. It shows, not the need to abolish capital punishment, but the need to have an adequate appeal court system, one in which there is ready access to the highest courts of the land so that any person convicted of a capital crime will be able to appeal that sentence and have the trial reviewed in such a way that the highest courts of the land will be satisfied that he had a truly fair hearing when his trial was conducted. It shows, secondly, the need for having some provision for non-capital murder so that any acts of homicide will not lead to a charge of capital murder, unless there is no doubt about the guilt of the person convicted of that murder. Where there is any doubt, certainly where there is any reasonable doubt because a conviction would rest upon circumstantial evidence, there should be provisions for non-capital murder so that the person, if convicted unjustly, would not be executed but would still have the opportunity to have that sentence reversed.
I am saying these things should be, but I recognize, as do all hon. members, that we already have these things; we already have an appeal court system. We already have legal aid throughout the land so that any citizen can have access to the highest courts. We already have provision in the Criminal Code for non-capital murder. In recommending to the House that Bill C-2 be defeated, we are not asking that capital punishment be provided for in the Criminal Code but rather that we return to the 1961 system in which a distinction was made between capital and non-capital murder. At that time a capital murder charge was reserved for those acts of homicide where the evidence led one to believe that the accused committed murder willfully, and with some premeditation.
Under that system we recognized the desirability of having the charge of non-capital murder brought against the accused in cases where there was some doubt, or where the presumption of guilt rested on circumstantial evidence; where there was no premeditation, where homicide took place as the result of an impulsive action, the so-called crime of passion.
The further argument brought before us is that capital punishment does not deter. The evidence for saying this rests on the fact that in the states where capital punishment is part of the legal system there are still murders. I point out that those states represent most of the member

nations of the United Nations. That argument is brought forward by many abolitionists as though it were a great revelation, as though it were the final argument to be made, as though there were nothing more to be said. The point we must recognize is that regardless of what penalty we have for murder, or for that matter for any other crime, there will always be some instances of the crime being committed.
If it is logical to say that we are going to abolish capital punishment because in countries where it exists people still commit murders, we could use the same argument to say that we are going to abolish penitentiaries, simply because in our country people are still robbing banks and committing other crimes. People have been committing these crimes for years, and have not been deterred from committing them by prison sentences.
We are submitting that capital punishment has validity since some people are deterred from committing homicide because of the presence of the capital punishment threat in the Criminal Code. We are also suggesting that the growth of the rate of homicide in Canada since the de facto abolition of capital punishment is evidence of the contrary being the result, that capital punishment is in effect a deterrent, and that the lack of capital punishment is one reason why crimes of violence and homicide have increased and are increasing in our country.
A further argument put forward on this matter is that society is at fault, and that we should not bring down upon a single, helpless victim of social ills the final, supreme penalty of capital punishment. If I recall correctly, in his opening address on this bill the Solicitor General said that every murder represents a failure by society. This is an example of the kind of double talk that is permeating our whole thinking today.
Hon. members will recall the satire written in the late 1940's which visualized the world that was to come in 1984. The society that was to develop by 1984 was to be one in which the meaning of many words would be reversed, so that people would think freedom was slavery, war was peace, and so on. Once again we have an example of that confusion of language and thinking in the way some people are now prepared to suggest that when a murder is committed the murderer is not at fault, but the rest of us are. I suppose that, if we follow that through logically, we should all be punished in some way if we are the ones who are really guilty. But that is not suggested, Mr. Speaker. On the contrary, it is suggested that we should minimize the punishment for the person who committed the act.
I submit that our penitentiary system must rest on the belief in individual responsibility. The responsibility of the individual to give an accounting for his behavior is one of the fundamental beliefs of our society, of any civilized society. Unless the individual is responsible for his behavior, then we really cannot expect a society to have any moral foundation at all. We are submitting that the penitentiary system in Canada ought to have the character of individual responsibility as one of its foundation principles. We ought to say to a murderer who has willfully committed that crime, taking from another his most precious possession, life itself, "You are responsible for what you have done. You, having willfully taken the life of another, must be prepared to forfeit your own."
October 19, 1973

One of the things that impressed me on recently reading a book called "The Valacchi Papers" was the judgment of some friends of the mafia killer, Joe Valacchi, that "Joe believes everybody is to blame for Joe, except Joe." Are we not saying that over and over again in the way we are modifying, changing and adjusting our attitude to law enforcement? We are saying that everybody is to blame for a crime except the criminal. What we must insist upon once again is the need for society to say to the individual, who in effect is making war upon it, "You are responsible for what you have done."
The debate on Bill C-2, Mr. Speaker, has aroused more public interest than any other debate by parliament in this session. One reason for the widespread interest is that the people of Canada feel profoundly about the significance of the issue before us. The people of Canada are concerned not only with the letter of the legislation before us; they are concerned with the spirit that it expresses. As a parliament, we ought to ponder profoundly the message that is coming to Parliament Hill from every corner of Canada, the message which says that people want a firming up in the administration and enforcement of law.
People look upon this bill as symbolizing the attitude of Canadian society. One reason the majority of people oppose this bill is that it does not represent their attitude to law enforcement. People want a firmer, more just law enforcement than this bill provides. If parliament were really listening to the people of Canada it would resoundingly defeat this bill.
In the course of this debate there is one negative aspect of the discussion that has concerned many of us, and that is the way some members have imputed certain motives and certain deficiencies to others. There has been an easy assumption on the part of some of those who favour Bill C-2 and are thus abolitionists, that those who oppose it are blood-lusting sadists, red-necked, narrow-minded bigots who want revenge. On the other hand, those who have argued against Bill C-2 and are thus considered retention-ists, are sometimes inclined to think that those who support it are woolly-minded do-gooders, and so on. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, I think that both sides have come to the debate with honest, serious, heart-searching conviction. In this respect it has been a very good debate and expressive of the best character of parliament.
This House cannot take a decision which will satisfy everybody, but a debate which gives the opportunity to all to express their diverse views, as has this one, is a demonstration of the democratic process. I have welcomed the opportunity to address the chamber, and hope that in the course of the next few days a sufficient number of members will reach the decision that we should defeat this bill in order that the people of Canada may believe their parliament is truly and democratically trying to carry out the will of the people, clearly, forcefully and visibly expressed as that will has been.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
We have seen members of parliament stand in this House, go on radio and television and be interviewed by the media, saying, "I, personally, do not believe in capital punishment. I think it is a terrible thing to take another human life. But I have surveyed my riding, I have sent out a questionnaire and the results are conclusive and overwhelming; the majority of my constituents want capital punishment to be retained and therefore I shall have to vote against Bill C-2 and for the retention of capital punishment in all its aspects."
Mr. Speaker, I say to these people that they are doing one thing and one thing alone: they are putting their consciences up for sale. They are bidding for votes at the next election. If they truly believe that capital punishment is a bad thing, let them have the guts to stand up like men and women, state their positions, vote according to their positions and take the consequences next time the only real ballot that means anything is taken-that is, at the next election. Let them have the courage of their convictions and not hide behind this phony defence of a poll. In many instances the polls that I have seen ask, "Are you opposed, or not opposed, to capital punishment: yes or no?" Not any choice, not any option just-"Do you oppose, or favour, capital punishment: yes or no?" That is it. Those

October 19, 1973
Capital Punishment
polls are phony, Mr. Speaker. The only poll that counts is the poll taken on election day.
I have been accused of taking the position that I am going to vote against the will of my constituents because I have not taken any poll. I have not consulted my constituents on this matter, and I have no intention of doing so because I consulted them on October 30 last year. On that day last year, 55,024 votes were cast in Ottawa West and all but 245 were cast in favour of candidates who had publicly declared, in a record number of candidate meetings, some on television and radio and all reported in the local press and nationally-I cannot think of a riding in which more interest was shown by the media-and put themselves on record as opposing capital punishment and favouring Bill C-2.
There cannot be any doubt in my mind where my constituents stand on the issue, Mr. Speaker. There was over an 80 per cent turnout at the polls, and those who voted for me voted for a candidate who had publicly pledged himself to support a five-year extension of the legislation in existence, which is the idea that we now see embodied in Bill C-2. My Liberal opponent took the same position, as did my NDP opponent. The only one in favour of doing away with Bill C-2 and reinstating capital punishment was the Social Credit candidate who received those 245 votes.
If members are interested in polls or opinion-testing, attitudinal surveys or whatever you want to call them, I can tell about one which is more scientific than the ones used here, which are just drops in the ocean and touch one householder out of eight or nine voters. This survey was conducted by a man at the University of Western Ontario. I will not give his name because I have not been in touch with him to get his permission. He selected a sampling of people in the city of London, Ontario, who to his best knowledge and that of his associates made up a representative sampling of the people in that city. He sent out experienced interviewers. I will not go through all his findings, but here are his conclusions:
The most direct implication of the present study, however, is that some of the motives and characteristics associated with favouring the death penalty are inconsistent with important Canadian values and goals. Canadian people and institutions formally endorse the principles of humane legal justice, democratic as opposed to authoritarian values, and equality for all citizens. The present survey suggests that people who favour the death penalty, especially those who favour it most strongly, are likely to have characteristics which are anti-thetical to these values and goals: they are more likely than persons opposed to the death penalty to be seekers of vengeance and punishment, to hold authoritarian instead of democratic social and political beliefs, and to score high on measures of prejudice. These conclusions would seem worthy of consideration by political, governmental, and legal decision-makers; simply noting percentages in superficial public opinion polls is not enough.
I submit that, counter to the nineteenth century views expressed by many of the proponents of the return to the Dark Ages, the problem that the people of Canada face is not that of murder. There is no "Mack the Knife" around every corner, ready to stick a knife in your back. The people of this country do not go to bed worrying about being murdered in their beds. On the other hand, they are

concerned about the rising incidence of crimes against the human person which fall short of murder.
Let me quote some statistics in connection with Ottawa. I chose the month of August, 1973, at random. It is usually hot in August in Ottawa, and if there is ever a time when violent crimes or murder may be committed in this city, it is in August. There were no murders, no manslaughters and no attempted murders. There was one rape and ten other sexual offences. There were 89 assaults, and 17 robberies. In the year 1972 there were five murders, no manslaughters, one attempted murder, and 12 rapes; there were 145 other sexual offences, 18 woundings, 973 assaults, 184 robberies, and so on.
Our legal system provides stiffer jail sentences for stealing somebody's property than for beating that person half to death. I suggest that we need in this country a thoroughgoing review of the sentencing provisions of the Criminal Code, of the bail provisions, of weekend tickets of leave, parole and other associated provisions. I have said so to the Solicitor General personally and I have said it to him in writing. I believe that is the thing all the people of Canada have the right to be concerned about. The passing of a law that will give the state the right to execute another human being is not going to remove the legitimate fears of our citizens that they may be the victims of violence directed against the person which may fall short of murder.
I will give an example, right here in Ottawa. A few months ago a small store on St. Laurent Boulevard was held up. An innocent bystander was shot and killed in that robbery. Three men were arrested in connection with the robbery. Two of them at that time were out on bail for the offence of possessing a sawed-off shotgun. Actually, I believe the weapon was a sawed-off 22 caliber gun, which is of no use to anyone except for criminal purposes. I could not hit the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) from where I stand with a 22 caliber sawed-off gun, no matter how good my aim is. A gun like that is no good for target practice, no good for pest hunting and no good for anything except holding people up. And you can buy such a gun in any store that sells it so long as you have the $10, or whatever it takes, to buy it.
That people who were hauled in for possessing such a weapon should be turned loose on bail is incomprehensible. Those people were turned loose, just like the snap of a finger, on their own recognizance. I do not want to prejudice their trial and I will not mention any names. In fact, I do not know what has happened to the case. However, if it turns out that they are guilty, we ought to look at two choices-the return to capital punishment, or my suggestion that we pass Bill C-2 and concentrate on stricter bail laws and parole regulations. If we go back to the Dark Ages by resurrecting capital punishment, in the end three people will have been killed, the man who was shot in the store and the two men who will presumably hang for murder if they are found guilty.
If my formula had been followed, nobody would be dead because those men would not have been loose on bail to kill an innocent man, and they would not be executed. We call ourselves civilized, yet sometimes after listening to some speeches I wonder how civilized we are. I could think of a great many crimes for which we ought to
October 19, 1973

prescribe the rope, if we are to include murder as an offence punishable by death. I do not think we ought to kill anybody for anything. Several members who want to see Bill C-2 defeated have been almost Jesuitical in their arguments. They force reasonable people into a compromise position and then turn that compromise position against those people and say that is a reason for not adopting the principle at all.
Those of us who support Bill C-2 do so with reservations, of course. We do not believe that there should be capital punishment for any cause at all; but we are prepared to accept, under pressure, the idea that there may be a certain deterrent effect in the case of prison guards and police officers. And because we are trying to meet the legitimate objections of people who want to hang everybody in sight, what happens: they turn our own decency and our own middle of the road position back on us and try to make this into an argument for rejecting the whole thesis.
If we are to retain the rope, I can suggest a few more categories that might be included in the law. Let us bring to the gallows the directors of companies who run off with company assets, so causing the company to go bankrupt and pouring down the drain the savings of widows, pensioners and orphans. Send to the guillotine all governments that create half a million unemployed deliberately and so kill people, perhaps less quickly than by the gun but none the less effectively. To the guillotine with those people! Send to the guillotine landlords who charge extortionate rents. There is a whole list of people who commit crimes infinitely more harmful to our society than the killing of one human being.
The fact of the matter is that by far the majority of murders in this country, or crimes that are classed as murder, are the result of domestic disputes. Usually the victim is related in some way, often by marriage, to the executioner. The person who commits the crime is not a criminal; yet those people are referred to by certain hon. members as "those members of the criminal element" as though such murders were deliberately committed. They are not. They are committed by men and women who have been pushed too far, so they commit a crime. They are not criminals, and the purposes of our society are not served by their spending one day in jail. But there are other people who commit crimes of violence which fall short of murder. They, in my opinion, ought never again to see the light of day except in the exercise yard of a prison.
Everywhere I have gone in this country I have spoken to audiences that heretofore had been in favour of the reimposition of capital punishment. Everywhere I have gone, people have come up to me and said, "By God, that is a proposition that makes sense, because you are right." Murder is not the rule. It is crimes against the human person that we ought to fear. We punish more severely offences against property than we do crimes against the human person. As I said before, it is possible for a criminal to be given a stiffer penalty for stealing my car than for beating me unconscious. We glorify so-called athletes who batter each other around in the plain view of millions watching an NHL game on television. Those people are considered to be heroes. We do not prosecute them for causing bodily harm to one another; we applaud. We do
Capital Punishment
not censor our children's television programs to make sure that violence is removed from those programs, as we ought to do.
If the people of Canada are worried about anything, it is not that they are going to be murdered as a result of a meticulously carried out, exquisitely planned execution. What they are worried about is that they may be assaulted and robbed as they walk through the park at night, that their daughter may be raped, that their little child may be molested by a sex pervert, or that they or members of their family may be run down by a drunken driver. Those are all legitimate concerns.
I suggest this parliament would do much better to address itself, its energies and its time in meeting those legitimate concerns, to a proper review of sentencing, parole and bail regulations than by spending a great deal more time discussing whether it is right or wrong to kill a human being, regardless of what he or she has done, because there is only one answer to that proposition: it is wrong-and there is no way around that answer.
