speechtext:
I was involved in other matters. I may have misread the report. One member proposed an amendment that imprisonment be for 25 years. The minister did suggest a long prison term. The government wanted to get out of the whole concept of capital punishment but did not have enough nerve to bring it before the House. They were a bit disappointed with the original bill and wanted to change it when it got to committee. Fortunately, that change was not in order.
Rather than stand by their principles-and members may well ask, what principles-they decided to carry on with the bill in its present form. Even though the minister has admitted he does not believe in its principle, he still wants to press the bill through the House as a government bill. We have the strange situation where this government is trying to impose on the people of Canada a government bill that the government does not believe in and does not really want. The minister improperly tried to change it in committee. He did not have the guts to withdraw it and issue another bill calling for the complete abolition of capital punishment, if that is what he really wants.
As the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) said, we have a situation of "newspeak". If you are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment, under this bill you vote for capital punishment for those who murder police officers and prison guards; if you are against the abolition of capital punishment, you vote against capital punishment for those who murder police officers and prison guards. What "newspeak" this government has produced in the name of abolition! What "news-peak" this government is trying to press on Canada!
A lot has been said about constituency polls and what the people of Canada feel. This kind of thing goes on in Canada all the time. I have taken constituency polls by the usual mail-out. There is no question about it; they are not statistically accurate. However, a statistically accurate poll was carried out by students of the T. L. Kennedy secondary school at Mississauga. That was done with all

the finesse possible in the system of taking public opinion polls, by students who were studying and working on that matter. It showed in excess of 80 per cent of the people polled were in favour of capital punishment.
My own mail-out in December of last year, which I admit is not statistically accurate, showed 70 per cent of the people in favour of capital punishment. In September of this year, when the question was asked, "Do you support the complete abolition of capital punishment?" 88.6 per cent replied "No." When they were asked, "Do you support the bill as it now stands?" 89.1 per cent replied "No." You can say those polls are not accurate; you can say any poll is not accurate. As the hon. member for Ottawa West said, the only accurate poll is the one taken at election time. Several other hon. members had better realize that the only accurate poll is taken at election time.
If this issue were a key election issue on which the election of a party or a member would stand or fall, then I suggest those who vote for abolition of capital punishment in the "newspeak" method the minister has presented to this parliament will not return. These members do not trust the public of Canada. They think they are superior. They are superior to people who work in offices, to people who drive buses, to people who live in apartments, to people who really work for a living, because they sit in this great chamber and know better than their constituents how they should be treated. Perhaps we should throw out the entire judicial system which lets the jury decide. Perhaps we should let the superior men and women decide what is best for the poor public.
There are many issues in this country that the average person on the street may not be ready, willing and able to decide. That is why there are members of parliament. They examine issues across Canada, get the facts, and are given research facilities which the ordinary guy on the street does not have. This is why we are elected. Nevertheless, on an issue such as this, which is a clean question of: How, Mr. Citizen, do you want your Criminal Code written under which you and the rest of society are going to be governed?-between 80 and 90 per cent say they want to retain capital punishment in the Criminal Code. Only 1.1 per cent of the people in this poll are undecided on that question.
It is not a case where the evidence has not been put before the people of Canada. They have had the evidence before them for 10 or 15 years. These are people who are obligated to pay the penalty under the Criminal Code, as are we, and these people say, and say clearly, that they want a symbol-I say that this whole debate is totally symbolic-in our criminal jurisprudence that indicates that if a person commits a heinous murder, he pays for it with his life.
Before this bill comes to a final vote hon. members had better realize that this question is going to be an issue with people in the next election. The people of Canada expect their members to trust them, to look at their opinions seriously, instead of discarding them holus-bolus on the ground that those they represent do not have the ability to make up their own minds. I say members who vote against the opinion of the people of Canada had

better have some darned good explanations to give them. There is a demand in this society of ours for justice. Our society today is looking at the symbol of capital punishment to show that our Criminal Code means business.
A lot has been said about the right of the Crown to exercise the ancient right of clemency. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) suggested that that right of clemency has been available only to the rich and the privileged. That is the kind of remark one would expect from a member of his party. That is not at all the case. The prime minister has been exercising clemency in every case since 1962. This right of clemency, on recommendation to the Governor General, whether exercised properly or not, remains the prerogative of the Crown and has been a prerogative of the Crown since time immemorial.
The right of the Crown to exercise clemency, leniency and justice is inalienable. To suggest that it is used only for the benefit of the rich and the privileged is utter nonsense. Our people want a symbol in the Code that provides the maximum penalty for those who commit the most heinous, miserable and horrible crimes contemplated by the Code, including not only murder but treason. This provision of the maximum penalty must remain in our Code.
It is essential in this nation that our criminal law reflects the concepts and ideas of the people of Canada. The people of Canada, including our police forces, prison officials and public officials generally who are in charge of the administration of the Code say that the Code must have the respect of the people. Without this maximum penalty provision in the Code, the Code will not have the respect of Canadians. It is imperative that criminal laws which affect every one of us have our respect.
When we make criminal laws that do not reflect the mores of the society that governs us, we breed disrespect for those laws and for our judicial system. In the result, we hurt all of Canada. This bill and the votes on it are symbolic in that respect. Our system of law must respect the mores of the society it governs, and that society clearly demands that there be capital punishment. When we tell society to go away, that we will not give them capital punishment, we breed disrespect not only for the Criminal Code but for all our laws.
This is one of the reasons for the growth of violence and the growth of disrespect for moral issues shown throughout our society. Perhaps people are not respecting the law. Perhaps they say: Oh, it doesn't matter what the law says. Parliament can do what it wants. That is not the thing that should happen. Parliament must pass laws which reflect the mores, desires and will of the people it governs. This whole debate has turned into a symbolic thing and on that basis, if on no other, the bill must be defeated.
The past election has been referred to. I said there should be capital punishment for murderers of police officers, prison guards and perhaps for airline hijackers and paid killers. There has been a great deal of pressure, a great many speeches, a great many killings since that time. It has been pointed out to me that to say just hijackers, just paid killers, does not cover all of the
Capital Punishment
aspects of heinous, premeditated murder. It has been pointed out to me that the killing of a police officer may not be nearly as serious as the cold-blooded murder of young children. Yet the cold-blooded murderer of young children will go into our luxurious prison system from which he can probably escape if he wants to, and the person who happens to kill a police officer in a gun battle will hang. I have not hardened my views. I have said that we must better define what is a heinous, premeditated murder and provide for capital punishment in those cases.
It was my hope that when this bill went to committee there would be some real study, an honest attempt by the government to try to develop a position toward the Criminal Code which would bear some acceptance by the vast majority of Canadians. But we did not have that right. The government decided it was going to play hanky-panky with the committee, hanky-panky with the people of Canada and do what it wanted.
A great deal has been said about the question of deterrence. It is clear from the government's view of the bill that the government regards capital punishment as a deterrent, otherwise Bill C-2 would not have been presented to us. The government says that if we provide capital punishment for the murder of police officers and prison guards, that is sufficient deterrent. The question of deterrence has been raised by many. I refer hon. members to the whole Criminal Code system. The Criminal Code provides that if you commit a crime you receive a penalty, and the concept of the penalty is that it will deter others from committing the same type of crime. Therefore, for impaired driving we provide a minimum fine of $50 and a minimum three months' suspension on the first offence, and it does not take long before you face a minimum six months in jail or a minimum never drive agaiq penalty. All of us know this has deterred some of us from imbibing more than we might otherwise have done.
We come to the question of car theft, for example. We provide for a minimum sentence of one year. Perhaps it does not deter people from stealing cars, but it sure as heck has an effect when a case comes before the court, because there is another offence called joy-riding and there is a real attempt to reduce the charge from stealing because, they say, perhaps that sentence is too rough. Maybe the deterrence of capital punishment is too rough, but the people of Canada do not think so. I say to the minister that the Criminal Code is governing the people of Canada. He is not governing the people of Canada. He is not a dictator. The government is not a dictatorship yet.

I shall conclude what I have to say in two minutes. I thank hon. members for allowing me to do so. It is essential that we develop something to improve our society's mores, our society's attitude to life, our society's respect for law and indeed cut down the amount of violent crime and other offences that are occurring. A lot has been

Capital Punishment
said by members about the present penal system. We are not happy with it. A committee of this House has been touring the countryside looking at our penitentiaries, and I hope it will soon make a report to this House. One of the things I have heard from members of that committee is that the system is not working well. We are not in fact reforming some of the people who cannot be easily handled, and we are not keeping them under control as we should. Some people are pretty dangerous types and are pretty horrible types. With some people you begin to wonder whether they are people or not. So we have to do a great deal of work in prison reform. That is where the time of the House should be spent, not on this debate.
What we must do is build a more loving society and work on systems that can reform and change people. If there was ever an argument for capital punishment of those who commit heinous murder, the argument is this: the system does not protect us against a person murdering a second time. From the matter in which we have run our prisons, from the inability of our prison system to reform dangerous criminals, persons on the street who may fear for their lives are entitled to demand the protection which the death penalty gives.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that everything must have been said on capital punishment, judging by the number of debates we had and the length of speeches delivered on this subject. Many things have been said, but one surprised me particularly. Not a single hon. member cared to discuss the lot of the murder victim. We did not ask ourselves what we could do to save the life of the victim of a rape or of a kidnapping. We talked about parole, penitentiaries, in short about things which were not relevant at all to the amendment I had introduced.
Anyway, we talked about the value of life, but we did not say a word about the life of the person who has been assassinated. We have also said that capital punishment was not a deterrent and we proved it with several statistics. This proves absolutely nothing because no potential criminal or no confirmed criminal will come and say: I was prevented from assassinating someone because of capital punishment. It proves absolutely nothing. Yet, a criminal arrested recently boasted that he had killed 28 persons in different countries, some of them in the province of Quebec. With capital punishment, the lives of several of these victims would have been saved, including the lives of two fathers of several children; not a single word was said about it.
Here is the best proof that capital punishment is a deterrent: during recent weeks, we visited 15 penal institutions and all but four guards assured us that capital punishment was a deterrent because, for a prisoner sentenced to life imprisonment one or two murders do not make any difference; he is sentenced to life imprisonment in any case. This is proof it is a deterrent, particularly among prisoners.
In everyday life, no criminal will come and say he was prevented from killing because of capital punishment. A lot has been said, including some platitudes spoken a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly), but-

The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) when referring to my amendment said that what appears to be rape is the result of provocation or invitation. Let me refer to statistics. From 1961 to 1970, 86 women were killed as a result of sexual assault. Of these 86, 21 were under 15 years of age. So I ask the hon. member, where is the invitation or the provocation when a young girl of two, three or four years of age is involved?

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: Ask me about the 15 year-old ones.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
I am referring especially to young girls under 15 years of age. The hon. member for Broadview further mentioned that I had a certain hangup with regard to the crimes of kidnapping and rape, that there was an emotional involvement in my presenting the amendment and therefore it was difficult to be rational about it.
The hon. member evidently did not listen to my speech. I wonder where the irrationality is when I explained that the criminal act of kidnapping was a two-stage decision, and stressed this point particularly. There are two separate criminal acts in the case of kidnapping. Once the kidnapping is carried out, where the aim is ransom money or the liberation of a criminal, it is logical to assume that before the victim is put to death the death penalty will have a deterrent effect. It is only logical to think that. Anyone who is mentally unbalanced is never sentenced to death, anyway.
Another hon. member mentioned that in the United States capital punishment has been abolished. I have a little bit of news for him. I should like to remind this member, first, that a year ago after the Supreme Court outlawed capital punishment, the legislatures in 17 states introduced new laws to meet the objections raised by the Supreme Court. Second, Congress has a variety of bills aimed at overturning the Supreme Court's ruling. Third, President Nixon has called for legislation making capital punishment mandatory for certain federal crimes, including hijacking. So rather than capital punishment being abolished, it seems that some convicts will be sentenced to die in the electric chair or in the gas chamber.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) suggested that many rapes are committed under severe emotional stress when the accused is under the influence of liquor or drugs. I should like to remind the minister that when psychologists, psychiatrists and psychoanalysts testify to the effect that the individual is not in full possession of his faculties, this is always taken into consideration. I should like to repeat this-
[ Translation]
-that the ultimate goal of my amendment was mainly to prevent the murder of kidnapping and rape victims.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), who is not afraid to give her opinion and to express her convictions. I even wonder if she would not be more at ease among us Creditists, because when amendments to legislation as important as Bill C-2 are put to the vote and that this vote is said in the House, in the
October 19, 1973

newspapers, on radio and on television to be a free vote, I wonder if the purpose is not to laugh at the Canadian people; I wonder if it is not to mislead them to make them think that there is a free vote on the capital punishment issue.
I noticed yesterday-I do not wish to make any comments on the vote-that cabinet solidarity is a fact. Members representing constituencies which are completely opposed to the abolition of capital punishment rose to vote against the logical amendments that were before us, but they are ready to vote on third reading for the adoption of the bill as it is now. Besides, some members did not show up in the House to vote because there had been an agreement not to concur in the amendments in order that the government win its case as a result of the vote. That is exactly what occurred yesterday. There is only one solitary group, which has been following its policy since the beginning of this discussion, that is for five years, and it is the NDP members' group who are "against" the abolition of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: They are in favour of abolition!

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
They are in favour of abolition. Even Bill C-2 stipulates that, for another five year period, the extension of the law would have for result that murderers of a policeman or a prison guard would be likely to be sentenced to death.
Recently, that is on last May, in the Senate, the Hon. Paul Martin said, and I quote:
Honourable senators, on Tuesday last Senator Choquette asked me for information as to how many persons have been found guilty of murdering prison guards and police officers, and how many have been executed, since the passage of an act to amend the Criminal Code, Statutes of Canada 1967-68, Chapter 15.
The legislation was passed in 1968 but brought before this House in 1967.
The office of the Solicitor General has now advised me that six persons have been found guilty of such a murder and none has been executed. Four sentences were commuted, as follows:
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, murderers laugh in their sleeves when they see this. The hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) just mentioned a typical case, that of Mesrine, who has recently been recaptured in France. He boasted that he had killed at least 28 or 30 people and stated boldly: I am ready to kill others. He likes it. It is a sport for him. He is arrested in Canada, he escapes, he is recaptured, he escapes again; it is easier to get out of jail than to get in.
Mr. Speaker, Mesrine was caught again in France. He could easily earn his living: he was an architect. All he had in mind was to kill.
Another one with whom we put up until he killed four young children was a man named Dion, from Quebec City. The law did not deal with him. His own jail companions did: they executed him. Meddling with the law like that does not make any sense. Mr. Speaker, I heard some New Democrats say: In developed and civilized countries, the death penalty has been abolished. However, in all socialist countries of the world, the death penalty is still in force. The death penalty is there.
Members of the New Democratic Party should go to Cuba and try to oppose Castro, and let them tell me whether the death penalty does not exist there. They should go to Morocco and see whether there is no death penalty. There is not even a trial. Let them go to Russia and oppose the communist government to see whether they will put up with them. Let them go to China from where our Prime Minister has just returned. The firing squad speeds up things over there.
Mr. Speaker, I hear the New Democrats speak of civilized countries-but is killing young children civilized? As stated by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), little girls of seven, eight and nine years old are the victims. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said: When they are older than 15, they may have made advances, but not those of 7, 8 or 9. It is mere bestiality on the murderer's part.

The two other cases, in which the trial courts registered convictions and passed sentences of death, are still before the courts. One of these cases is before the Quebec Court of Appeal and the other will be before the Supreme Court of Canada, if an extension of time is granted.
Mr. Speaker, after this legislation was passed, there were six convictions but no execution. I therefore wonder about the usefulness of such a law. Why are we discussing a piece of legislation if it is not complied with, if it is not applied? The government and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) favour the total abolition of capital punishment. That is exactly what we are doing right now. The provisions of the law are not followed and we are about to renew for five years this same law, which condemns and commutes sentences. Commutations follow condemnations.
Everybody knows what a murderer is. We try to rehabilitate him, as the former Solicitor General said, who is now Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), but society does not want him anymore. This minister would not hire a released murderer. Myself, I would not hire one in my business. Then, what can a released murderer do? He only can keep on killing, committing armed robberies and doing as he did before being imprisoned, condemned and released.
Mr. Speaker, surveys have been conducted throughout Canada on the issue of capital punishment on which we will vote freely, maybe not this afternoon but probably Tuesday, because too many members will be absent Monday.
Some ministers who are strongly opposed to the abolition of capital punishment will have to vote for it. They will have to explain away their action to their constituents.
But all sorts of organizations are opposed to the abolition of capital punishment. For instance, my friends from the New Democratic Party-

Is that freedom?

Mr. Speaker, that is just about the most stupid question I ever heard, but anyhow, supposing that it is intelligent, I suggest that everyone of my colleagues of the Social Credit party will freely give him a personal answer, without having consulted me concerning capital punishment. The same is true of us.

Prove it.

Sure, and I would be pleased to do so. Mr. Speaker I was saying that we are receiving comments on Bill C-2 even from labour organizations, and my friends of the NDP are experts in union matters. I have here a letter received from the Brotherhood of Railway, Airline & Steamship Clerks, Freight Handlers, Express and Station employees. There is absolutely no doubt that NDP members know these organizations. I have a copy of this letter that was sent to the right hon. Prime Minister. I quote:
During a regular meeting, it was resolved to inform you that Local # 2303 is in favour of the retention of Capital Punishment". We hope to receive your comments on the retention or the abolition of this penalty. On behalf of the members of our Local # 2303, X remain

R. De Lorme, Chairman.
In another part of the province, namely in Sept-Iles, a kind of referendum or public opinion poll was carried out

by the Chamber of Commerce, and very clear questions were asked. I quote;
I support the abolition of capital punishment.
Yes: 51; No: 300
I support the retention of capital punishment as applied before. Yes: 295; No: 33.
According to you, has the number of murders increased in Canada during the past five years?
Yes: 316; No: 23.

And what people did not know either is that California reinstated the death penalty a few days ago, and it was the last state to accept legislation to abolish the death penalty.
How old are you?
The average age of those polled was 34.
So do not tell me those are aged people or kids; these are ordinary people stating their point of view. And at the end of the letter we are told by the Chamber of Commerce:
Please send your early reply to the Sept-Iles Chamber of Commerce .. .
This is a local Poll. For some it is a matter of religion. I must say that I received more letters against the abolition of the death penalty from Protestant ministers than from Catholic priests. But I have been reading Catholic news reports and an article of a magazine called Aujourd'hui Quebec which is constantly quoting St. Thomas d'Aquinas and I quote;
So, said St. Thomas "although it is bad to take the life of a man keeping his dignity as a reasonable human being and sacred person ..., to take the life of the sinner (that is to say he who through a serious sin has lost his sacred character) may be a good thing."
This is the point of view of an undisputably competent philosopher. Once more about capital punishment, the director of the magazine Rev. Guy Poisson stated and I quote;

It was recently suggested by abolitionists that in countries where the death penalty had been abolished the crime rate had not increased. Their adversaries stated the contrary. In my opinion those are simplistic views because at the same time we should study all other factors liable to increase or decrease the number of offenses and among others:
the organization of work and leasure, standards of living, the police force, the multiplication and control of liquor stores, etc ... And then, all those who have been dissuaded from committing a crime through fear of capital punishment are not boasting about it.
The hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) referred to it a while ago. The article goes on:
October 19, 1973

This debate on capital punishment retained the whole country's attention following the sad stories of Victor Spencer and Gerda Munsinger. We are informed that representations will soon be made to ask Parliament to legalize abortion.
What will'then be the Prime Minister's position? Will he invite members of Parliament to vote "ACCORDING TO THEIR CONSCIENCE"?
Will those who appealed to sentiments to protect life touch the same sensitive chord to prevent the murdering of innocents? Or will they maintain that God remains the absolute master of life?
Mr. Speaker, we receive comments from almost everywhere against the abolition of capital punishment.
I have here a letter from Mr. Rene Bilodeau, from Sherbrooke, who conducted a survey in that city and I quote:
.. . report on a survey on capital punishment involving 100 persons, 30 years and over, all walks of life; 77 for capital punishment, 7 undecided, 16 against. General comment: why should we reward a murderer who now costs $10,000, keeping him in a warm place, well fed, with medical care, T.V. etc., and denying a pension to eight applicants of 60. I am 59, victim of asbestosis .. .
That man does not get any pension while murderers have security.
Mr. Speaker, as I said it is not because we are vindictive men that we are retentionnist. For instance, hijackers constitute a real danger for thousands of lives. If capital punishment had been invoked for those individuals, 90 per cent of hijackings would have been avoided. In several places, the number of murders would have decreased instead of increasing as is the case now. Every morning when I glance at a newspaper, I can read on the front page: One, two, three murders have been committed last night. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) says: On behalf of humanity, we must save the murderers' lives. If we condemn them to death, that will not prevent other murderers from continuing their activities. One thing is sure: When we hang a murder, he will stop killing. That is a sure thing, but the law maintaining capital punishment constitutes a barrier, a fence, everybody knows that. If you go over it, if you plunge, if you go beyond, you fall into an abyss. For the one who does not want to be hanged, the only thing to do is to refrain from it. Everybody is on an equal footing before this legislation.
Indeed we sincerely believe that this legislation should be replaced by the one in force previously, but which was improved, and under which we would be given the assurance that should there be any uncertainty, small as it might be, the convict would be given the benefit of the doubt and, we would not take the risk of a miscarriage of justice by imposing hanging in a doubtful case.
There have been and, there still are such cases in Canada. Therefore, it is sufficient to avoid passing such sentence-

-to reinstate the death penalty in Canada, and at the same time, I am flabbergasted to see the attitude of the

minister who lives in Montreal, where 90 percent of the people are in favour of maintaining the death penalty. And the minister has the nerve to tell us that the Canadian people want the abolition of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, the solution is simple. At election time, why not write the following simple question on the ballot: for or against death penalty, throughout Canada, you will see the reaction. It is being said that the government is killing people by the people for the people. A democratic government must take into account the views and the will of the people. What is happening to that democracy at the present time? We fall into the trap, we play the game of those who wish to have murders committed in Canada. We are scared of taking position. For what reason? Under whose influence? I do not know.
As for us, we are surely expressing the will of the electors not only of our constituencies, but of the whole of the province and of the whole of Canada on the death penalty issue. I am coming back to what I was saying at the beginning. In several countries, rather strange executions are performed.
When the military junta took over in Chile and confined some 7,000 persons in a football stadium, the members of the New Democratic Party cried shame.
It was totally unacceptable for those bad rightists to crush leftists in Chile. But the New Democrats did not object when students in Czechoslovakia tried to recover part of their freedom that consisted only in putting down their ideas, in writing, not revolting against the regime but only writing down what they thought.
Mr. Speaker, the Soviet army was called in to crush those students. In 1956, Hungary wanted to recover part of its freedom and was literally crushed by the Soviets. Did we hear the NDP protest against that? No. That was all right.
In all countries where there has been bloody revolutions this is the way things happened. But when rightists in Chile returned to power under arms, Mr. Speaker, how unfortunate, scandalous, frightening it is all. The Parliament of Canada is being asked to pass a resolution condemning the army in Chile. But let us not condemn Cuba, or any of the communist or leftist countries in the world. When I hear people reason like that, I wonder what would become of Canada if we ever had a socialist government.
Mr. Speaker, we are lucky to still have in Canada the freedom to face one another, to tell one another what we think, some thing that does not exist in several countries presently, Thanks to British freedoms, we have that right. We have the right to oppose government members. We have the right to talk against Tories, NDP members in the same way they have the right to talk against us. That is freedom. The day we lose it there will be tears shed, tears of blood, to reconquer that freedom. Mr. Speaker, we want that freedom for everybody. We want it for murderers but we also want it so that before a murderer commits his crime, some law will stop him from going ahead, under the penalty of paying for it. Then there might not be so many murderers and order would prevail. It would be more respected in Canada and, naturally, there would be more justice. Some economic and social conditions incite people

to revolt. Then, they lose their head and can be provoked into killing.
So let us establish social, economic and political standards of justice that will enable man to fulfil himself. In doing so, we will finally create a better balanced society where it will be good to live, a society which will characterize the finest country of all, Canada.

Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes I wish to reiterate some of the views expressed on second reading of this bill. As I listened to the speeches on second reading, and now on third reading, I felt a deep regret that so often we have to approach this subject from an emotional point of view. Some seem to think that others have not given full consideration to the question. The abolitionists seem to feel they are the only ones living in the twentieth century. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. I believe every member of the House has looked at this question very seriously from both sides and has reached a reconciliation with his conscience.
If an hon. member's conscience happens to agree with the generally held views of his constituents, then he is not subjected to the tyranny of the opinion poll: his conscience is in agreement with the views of the constituents he represents. There are times when individual members will vote contrary to the generally held opinions of their constituents. If a member says in this House that he is in favour of retention, and that his view happens to be shared by the majority of his constituents, that does not mean in any way that there has been any tyranny of any opinion poll or that there is any reflection on his conscience. It does not mean that he is playing politics or that he is simply doing what the general public wants him to do.
Having looked at this question closely, I have distinguished between premeditated and non-premeditated murder. As I said in the debate on second reading, I would not support the death penalty in cases involving nonpremeditated murder. A number of abolitionist speakers have said that many murders are domestic matters; they are not premeditated and, therefore the death penalty should not be invoked. I think many retentionists agree with that position. But there is another type of murder, Mr. Speaker-premeditated, wanton murder in which a person cold-bloodedly calculates taking the life of another person. That type of wanton, cold-blooded murder must be punished with the supreme punishment which we are discussing today in this debate on Bill C-2.
Nothing in history shows that a democracy is measured by the yardstick of whether or not capital punishment is invoked. The strength of a democracy and of a government lies in its ability to protect the freedoms and rights of all its citizens. It does not depend on whether a democracy is liberal in its thinking, or whether we are free thinkers. Democracy is not bom of weakness and is not exercised from weakness. A democracy is only as strong as its individual citizens. It is strong only so long as the government representing the individual wishes of the citizenry is willing to back up the freedoms which are our right. Those freedoms can exist only if we all obey the law. It is the
October 19, 1973

inherent responsibility of government to maintain the laws of a society and to punish those members who disobey the law. You cannot escape punishment for wrongdoing. Often we consider that punishment for crime is mere retribution. It is not retribution; it is justice.
There is one other point I want to put on record. The case I will mention took place in Manitoba not long ago. It is now before the courts. I will not dwell on it except to say that it involves an 11 year old girl who was sexually molested and left to die. When you meet brutal cases like that you must look at this issue squarely and consider your position on capital punishment.
Why is it that some people who are brought to court are given seven to eight years imprisonment on reduced charges? How soon are they paroled? Actually, Mr. Speaker, capital punishment for premeditated murder is not retribution; it is justice. It has been that way since time immemorial. This is at the back of the principles which this country has upheld for years. I urge all members of the House to seriously reconsider the question of premeditated murder. The only penalty that will bring justice in that situation, if there is justice, is capital punishment.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before addressing myself to the business at hand I ought to begin by saying that we have wasted enough time debating the question of whether or not the life of the murderer is worthier of consideration than other serious problems facing our nation.
I congratulate the movers of the amendments we voted on last night, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) and the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), for having brought those amendments forward. I was glad to support the amendments, and sorry they did not pass. However, the will of the House prevailed and that is part of the working of our democratic system. That system has been protected so long by our penal code which we have found beneficial in the past. Part of that code has involved down the years the maintenance of capital punishment as the supreme deterrent, of which I am a supporter.
The members of this House know, my constituents know and I want the Canadian people to know that I am a retentionist on this question. I am a retentionist because I believe that any corporate nation or state should always retain the right to demand the life of any citizen for capital crime. I believe that this ultimate deterrent should not be abandoned. I forget how many times I have spoken on this topic. I recall that I spoke last in support of capital punishment on May 23 of this year. Several months have passed since then. I must say that it appears the issue of capital punishment has taken precedence over the important issues that we should be trying to resolve.
I listened with interest to the speeches made this afternoon. I note that the NDP member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) said that the issue of capital punishment has been blown up out of all proportion. I believe I am quoting him correctly. I challenge him on that statement. He also said that some of us are out of step with the world community. I also challenge him on that statement. I employ a recent report of March 16, 1973, to do with the
Capital Punishment
United Nations, the highest and only authority of our world community. The report reads in part:
New forms of terror and violence are provoking countries to revert to the death penalty, still favoured by the majority of people and governments, a U.N. study said yesterday ...
The study said that opinion polls made both in countries which have abolished the death penalty and in those which retain it, show a majority of people favouring it.
So many speeches have been made on this subject, Mr. Speaker, that it would be difficult at this point for one to avoid repeating previous remarks. There is also the possibility that one may repeat statements made by other speakers. I noted that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) berated the tyranny of public opinion. I remind him of the headline in today's Toronto Star which says that it is foolish to underrate public opinion polls. The hon. member for Ottawa West does not like the tyranny of what he calls public opinion. I prefer that tyranny, if it can be termed as such, to the tyranny of lawlessness and anarchy which has so filled the Canadian people with revulsion that they now demand a strong deterrent and retribution in cases involving capital crime.
This is the same Liberal government that was in power when parliament approved the present five-year partial ban on capital punishment. It was the will of parliament during that five-year period that anyone convicted of capital murder would suffer the death penalty. It is implicit in the present law that capital murder is defined as the murder of a policeman or prison official while such an official is considered to be on duty. This is a fine distinction since it has always been considered that a policeman is on duty 24 hours a day. Leaving that aside, the fact is there have been a number of such murders in which it has been demonstrated that the officials killed were in fact acting in the line of duty.
Many members who were sitting in this House during the debate on the bill introduced in 1967 will remember the government's insistence that valuable data on the working of this law would be available to us at the end of the five-year period. Data was to be available to assist us in making up our minds whether capital punishment limited to these cases was in fact a deterrent to the murder of policemen. It has been stated over and over again during this debate that there is no such data. We do not have the valuable data the government insisted would be available to us. As we well know, the government has flouted this law, the law they wanted so much to have parliament approve. The partial ban on capital punishment was not an opposition motion; it was the brainchild of the government: it was they who fought to have it approved and implemented.
Speaker after speaker on the government side in 1967 called for the execution of murderers of policemen, calling policemen the guardians of public life and prosperity. Now we have the government backing off from their brainchild. In fact, they started backing off as soon as the original bill was enacted into law. There is clear evidence at this point that the government never intended to live up to the will of parliament. No clearer evidence is needed than the fact that every convicted murderer of a policeman has had the death sentence commuted by the cabinet since that act

October 19, 1973
Capital Punishment
came into force. The Canadian people are watching the government's pattern in giving dispensation with regard to the murder of Constable Maitland in Toronto.
It has been pointed out by many of my colleagues in this House that the government has in fact opted for total abolition of the death penalty. In taking this stand the government has not only abdicated its responsibility with regard to parliament's expressed will in this matter but it has also chosen to ignore the weight of public opinion. It has long been known that the great majority of Canadian people favour some form of capital punishment for capital crimes. I cannot in good conscience adopt a position on this matter that does not take into account the wishes of my constituents.
Parliamentarians in Canada, Great Britain and possibly some other countries delight in quoting the great parliamentarian Edmund Burke. There is no doubt that when Burke was in his prime in the 1770s he was among the greatest parliamentary orators. On at least one occasion Burke said that while he was always cognizant of the majority opinion of his constituents, he did not feel bound to act in accordance with majority opinion in all cases. The present government appears to carry this to the opposite extreme. They do not feel the majority opinion carries any weight at all.
It is this attitude by the government that is holding up settlement of the issue of capital punishment. I cannot accept this attitude, especially in light of a general breakdown of law and order in Canada today and the concern of millions of law-abiding Canadians that their interests are not placed above those who hold our laws and institutions in contempt.
When speaking in this debate last summer, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Beattie) noted that some people argue that capital punishment cannot be justified on the ground that the execution of a murderer does not bring the victim back to life or ease the burden of grief borne by the victim's family. He said that the act of murder should carry a price as high as the value of the life taken. To carry it a logical step further, the same people might argue that putting an arsonist in jail for burning a house does not restore the house to its original state.
I do not believe that the state should be denied the power and the right to exact the death penalty whenever it is thought by responsible people that extreme measures are needed to correct an intolerable situation. In my opinion, the recent rash of murders of policemen across Canada is an intolerable situation.
Some strange and interesting stories are told and written about in the anals of crime and punishment. One such story is said to have occurred in revolutionary Russia in the year 1920. The government of that time abolished capital punishment for a while, giving the reason that capital punishment was a bourgeois institution. During a meeting of the revolutionary council, one member announced angrily that a prominent general had been sentenced to death for treason while state law forbade the sentence of death. Another member leaped up and said the general had not been sentenced to death but had only been sentenced to be shot. That apparently satisfied the council. Such is the case in oriental countries today. That great and respected civilization for which the Prime Minister (Mr. 
Trudeau) has so much admiration, the Chinese, still practice capital punishment in a very stringent manner. When they deem it necessary, they line people up against a wall and shoot them.
The point I am trying to make is that many of those who plead the case for abolition are only trying to get out of making a decision that may be unpopular, or a decision that may cast them in the role of executioner. Abolitionists in my riding have said to me, "You are a retentionist. Would you be the executioner?" No, I would not be the executioner. The majesty of the Canadian people would be the executioner. In a civilized society such as ours, those of us in parliament must at some point accept the fact that some of our decisions are going to be difficult. I cannot cast my vote in favour of the murderer, and ignore the victim and the victim's family because my decision might label me as an executioner. I must be prepared to accept this eventuality, and so must every other member of this House.
Should a judge hesitate to sentence a dangerous and deranged criminal to penitentiary for life because some people feel that even animals should not be caged? Should a judge hesitate to pass sentence because the person sentenced will be denied the pleasures of the society that he has rejected and rebelled against? I cannot accept such logic, or absence of logic because I feel too strongly that the chief responsibility of parliament is to the millions of law-abiding Canadians. As legislators, we are denied the luxuries of vacillating and equivocating that are the privilege of some other spheres of activity.
We cannot abondon our responsibility to the majority of Canadians, using the thesis that life is sacred and that not even the state has the right to take a human life. The state does have that right. Capital punishment is an instrument of the state, and while it should be used only in the last resort, and while every avenue of appeal should be readily available to any who are sentenced to death, that right must be provided to the state.
The present government's policies of permissiveness, coupled with the ipso facto absence of the death sentence provided for in Canadian law for capital crime, are already showing their potential as a threat to organized society in Canada. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain also noted in his speech in this debate that there have been recent cases of policemen being shot and killed while investigating minor crimes, one case involving a relatively minor traffic offence. This is an indication that something is drastically wrong and it is time for those who plead the sanctity of human life to plead for the lives of the victims of violent, senseless crime.
Like most other members of this House, Mr. Speaker, I was appalled when the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) in July attempted to influence the standing committee to accept an amendment to abolish the death penalty completely. I know that I should not address myself at length to the committee hearings on this bill, but I wanted to make the point that this government in fact tipped its hand as far as its attitude to capital punishment is concerned. It also indicated that its old arrogance has not been abandoned at all; it has only been kept under wraps.
October 19, 1973

In light of the electoral position in this country today, just give this government another majority like it had before and it will be worse than ever.
In the absence of any clear proof to the contrary, we have been prepared to accept the view that the cabinet commuted each death sentence passed in the last five years on its own merits and that this was not a calculated thing, a case of government policy. Now we find that the government in fact wants total abolition. No other case can be made for the actions of the government in the past few weeks, and like some of my colleagues I must ask, why did the government not table a bill that called for abolition? I would like to know the reason, but unless enought of my colleagues also want to know, then we will be kept in the dark.
I would like to say at this point, Mr. Speaker, that last night I supported the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert. While I accept the argument advanced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that rape and murder would both have to be proved and that this would be virtually impossible, I would still like to see in the law such a provision as that proposed by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert. It should be in the law if only for its possible, and probable, deterrent value.
To sum up my remarks and my feelings on this matter we are debating, I must say that I cannot vote in favour of the bill now before the House. As I have said many times before, the bill as it now reads will do nothing in the way of providing protection to the law-abiding Canadian citizen against those who resort to violent crime as a way of life. It will not ensure that proper punishment will be exacted for the crime of capital murder. I know that there are people today who claim that our objective in this matter is not to punish, but until we are able to develop an utopian society where punishment as such does not enter into the scheme of things, then we must continue to punish wrongdoers. No one has come up with a better solution to a very serious problem and we are faced with a problem of major proportions.
I have always regarded myself as a realist and I cannot in good conscience approve of theoretical solutions to a real problem. It should be obvious to anyone that we cannot apply utopian theory to the very real problem of violent crime and brutal murder. I cannot believe that anyone elected to parliament to serve the interests of a constituency would come here and ignore the wishes of the majority of his constituents on a matter as serious as capital murder and violent crime.
My colleague the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) has sent members the result of a questionnaire that he mailed to his constituents, and these figures pretty
Capital Punishment
well match those from my own riding of Frontenac-Len-nox and Addington and from other ridings. They show that 88.6 per cent of the constituents polled in Peel South oppose abolition of capital punishment, and 89.1 per cent are opposed to the bill we are now debating. Most Canadians appear to want capital punishment reinstated as a penalty for murder, not because they have a taste for blood but because they would like at least to have us try something more drastic in our struggle against rampant lawlessness. They hope, I am sure, that the deterrent value of capital punishment will at least prevent some of the violent crimes and some of the murders.
I have said, and many of my colleagues have said, that we appear to be paying more heed to the sanctity of the life of the murderer than to the sanctity of the life of the murder victim. Let us put this matter back into perspective. Let us offer at least as much protection to the victim as to the criminal. It is not my responsibility to berate the government every time it commutes a lawful death sentence for brutal murder, and it is not for me to insist that the government live up to its responsibility under Canadian law and allow the decision of the courts to stand in respect of the death penalty. This bill has been proven to be total abolition of the death penalty inasmuch as the government has commuted every death sentence imposed in the past six or seven years for the murder of policemen.
I am not a vindictive man, and to my knowledge no one has ever suggested that I am bloodthirsty. However, my concern is more for the innocent victim of crime than for the criminal; therefore, I cannot support a bill that does not provide that measure of protection to which the victim is entitled. In conclusion, I am confident that if every member votes on this bill as his constituents feel on this question, as judged by surveys and questionnaires, the bill will not be passed by this House.
